title: I2C: master sends the address byte. Who sends the ACK?
options: The master, to say the byte was sent
The slave with that address, by pulling SDA low
Every slave on the bus together
explain: The slave that owns the address pulls SDA low for one clock: 'I am here'. No ACK (NACK) means no such device. An I2C scanner uses exactly this: it tries all 128 addresses and lists who answered.

title: LCD backpack SDA/SCL wired to D4 and D5 on the Uno. The LCD stays blank. Why?
options: D4 and D5 are normal GPIO. Uno hardware I2C is only on A4 (SDA) and A5 (SCL)
explain: Hardware I2C is wired to fixed pins: A4 = SDA, A5 = SCL on the Uno. D4/D5 have no I2C unit, so nothing talks and nothing ACKs. There is no error, just silence. A scanner would find 0 devices.

title: Simulated LCD row. You show 10, then 9. What does the row show?
explain: The LCD does not clear cells by itself. Writing '9' changes only column 0. Column 1 still holds '0' from '10', so you see 90. Print the number then pad with spaces, or write '9 '.

title: After 0 the LCD looks fine, but the I2C bus is busy all the time. Tap the bug.
explain: When i == 0 this branch runs on every loop(): thousands of I2C transfers per second for the same text. Print BOOM! once, on the tick that reaches 0, or use a flag/state so it runs one time.

title: LCD address 0x27 (7 bit). What are the first bytes on the wire for a write and a read?
explain: The first byte is the 7-bit address shifted left by 1, plus the R/W bit: 0 = write, 1 = read. 0x27 << 1 = 0x4E, so write = 0x4E and read = 0x4F. Arduino Wire takes the 7-bit form and does the shift for you.

title: lcd.begin() takes 40 ms inside setup(). prev stays 0. When does the first 1000 ms tick come, counted from the end of setup()?
explain: millis() is already 40 when loop() starts, and prev is 0. The first tick comes at millis = 1000, which is 960 ms after setup() ended. Fix: set prev = millis() at the end of setup().

title: UART 9600 baud, 8N1. The RX buffer holds 64 bytes. loop() is blocked. After about how many ms is it full?
explain: One byte = 10 bits (start + 8 data + stop). At 9600 bit/s that is 960 bytes/s, so 64 bytes take 64 * 10 * 1000 / 9600 = 66 ms. A delay(100) can lose incoming bytes.

title: The command parser gets garbage when the PC sends nothing. Tap the bug.
explain: Serial.read() returns -1 when no byte is waiting. Without Serial.available() the loop stores -1 (0xFF) again and again, and n++ also overruns buf[16]. Check available() first and guard n < sizeof buf - 1.

title: Serial Monitor sends "on" + CR LF. Your parser stops at '\n'. Does strcmp(buf, "on") == 0 match? (prints 1 if yes)
explain: Stopping at '\n' leaves the '\r' in the buffer: buf = "on\r". strcmp sees a different string. Ignore '\r' or trim it before the compare. Serial Monitor can send NL, CR, both or none.

title: Serial commands on a 2 KB Uno: 4 rules
bullets: Read with available() > 0, one byte at a time. read() gives -1 if empty.
Use a fixed char buf[] and an index. Check n < size - 1 before every store.
No String class (heap fragmentation) and no readString() (waits up to 1 s like delay).
End of command is '\n'. Also ignore '\r', the Serial Monitor may send both.
